newsitem.title: USA: U.S. applauds WTO ruling on Canada magazine laws.
newsitem.headline: U.S. applauds WTO ruling on Canada magazine laws.

text.p: The U.S. government on Monday hailed a World Trade Organization ruling against Canadian magazine laws, which Washington said discriminated against American publishers.

"The Canadian magazine practices we challenged greatly restrict the ability of our industry to compete in Canada," U.S. Trade Represenative Charlene Barshefsky said. She said the United States was "gratified" by the ruling of the WTO appellate body.

"This case makes clear that WTO rules prevent governments from using 'culture' as a pretense for discriminating against imports," Barshefsky said. "We look for prompt action by Canada to bring its magazine regime into compliance with its international obligations."

The case involved a 1995 Canadian law that imposed an 80 pecent tax on advertising in U.S. magazines that publish editions in Canada. The law was aimed at so-called split runs by Sports Illustrated magazine, published by Time Warner Inc.

The appellate body upheld a dispute-settlement panel's decision in March that said the tax violated international trade laws. It also overturned the panel's decision on Canada's practice of charging higher postal rates for magazines not produced in Canada by Canadian-owned companies.
The panel had found the practice consistent with global trade rules, but the WTO appellate body overturned that decision and found in favor of the United States.
U.S. officials saw the Canadian laws as a matter of discrimination against foreign products rather than cultural protection.

"You often find countries talk culture but act in ways that are clearly discrimatory with regard to trade," said one U.S. official. "This was an example of discrimination against foreign companies and periodicals under the name of culture but not in a manner that was consistent with how domestic providers would be treated."
Earlier Monday, Canadian Heritage Minister Sheila Copps said her government would look closely at the ruling and assess its options.
